17 Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data

17.3 Do It Yourself

Code 
pacman::p_load(scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes,
               gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table,
               CGPfunctions, ggHoriPlot, tidyverse)

17.4 Plotting Calendar Heatmap

17.4.2 Importing the data

Code 
attacks <- read_csv("Data/eventlog.csv")

17.4.3 Examining the data structure

Code 
kable(head(attacks))
timestamp source_country tz
2015-03-12 15:59:16 CN Asia/Shanghai
2015-03-12 16:00:48 FR Europe/Paris
2015-03-12 16:02:26 CN Asia/Shanghai
2015-03-12 16:02:38 US America/Chicago
2015-03-12 16:03:22 CN Asia/Shanghai
2015-03-12 16:03:45 CN Asia/Shanghai

17.4.4 Data Preparation

Code 
make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts, 
                        tz = tz[1], 
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
}
Code 
wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday', 
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday', 
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday', 
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp, 
                   .$source_country, 
                   .$tz)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))
Code 
kable(head(attacks))
tz source_country wkday hour
Africa/Cairo BG Saturday 20
Africa/Cairo TW Sunday 6
Africa/Cairo TW Sunday 8
Africa/Cairo CN Sunday 11
Africa/Cairo US Sunday 15
Africa/Cairo CA Monday 11

17.4.5 Building the Calendar Heatmaps

Code 
grouped <- attacks %>% 
  count(wkday, hour) %>% 
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
geom_tile(color = "white", 
          size = 0.1) + 
theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
coord_equal() +
scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "yellow", 
                    high = "red") +
labs(x = NULL, 
     y = NULL, 
     title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )

17.4.6 Building Multiple Calendar Heatmaps

Code 
top4_countries <- attacks %>%
  count(source_country, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 4) %>%
  pull(source_country)

grouped_multi <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4_countries) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

grouped_multi <- grouped_multi %>%
  mutate(
    wkday = factor(
      wkday,
      levels = c("Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
                 "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday")
    )
  )

ggplot(grouped_multi,
       aes(x = hour,
           y = wkday,
           fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white",
            size = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ source_country, ncol = 2) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_x_discrete(
    breaks = 0:23,
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    name = "# of attacks",
    low = "lightblue",
    high = "darkblue"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day"
  ) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6),
    panel.spacing = unit(1.2, "lines")
  )

17.4.7 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps

Code 
attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
Code 
top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()

17.4.8 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps

Code 
ggplot(top4_attacks, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
  geom_tile(color = "white", 
          size = 0.1) + 
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue", 
                    high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +

     title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday and time of day") +

        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )

17.5 Plotting Cycle Plot

17.5.1 Step 1: Data Import

Code 
air <- read_excel("data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")

17.5.2 Step 2: Deriving month and year fields

Code 
air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`), 
                    levels=1:12, 
                    labels=month.abb, 
                    ordered=TRUE) 
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))

17.5.3 Step 4: Extracting the target country

Code 
Vietnam <- air %>% 
  select(`Vietnam`, 
         month, 
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)

17.5.4 Step 5: Computing year average arrivals by month

Code 
hline.data <- Vietnam %>% 
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))

17.5.5 Srep 6: Plotting the cycle plot

Code 
ggplot() + 
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year, 
                y=`Vietnam`, 
                group=month), 
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue), 
             data=hline.data, 
             linetype=6, 
             colour="red", 
             size=0.5) + 
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")

17.6 Plotting Slopegraph

17.6.1 Step 1: Data Import

Code 
rice <- read_csv("data/rice.csv")

17.6.2 Step 2: Plotting the slopegraph

Code 
library(tidyverse)

# Prepare data
rice_slope <- rice %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980)) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.numeric(as.character(Year))) %>%
  select(Country, Year, Yield)

# Convert to wide format
rice_wide <- rice_slope %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Year,
    values_from = Yield,
    names_prefix = "Y"
  )

# Manually adjust label positions to avoid overlapping
rice_wide <- rice_wide %>%
  mutate(
    left_y = case_when(
      Country == "Japan" ~ Y1961,
      Country == "Korea" ~ Y1961,
      Country == "Malaysia" ~ 22000,
      Country == "China" ~ 21000,
      Country == "VietNam" ~ 20000,
      Country == "SriLanka" ~ 19000,
      Country == "Indonesia" ~ 18000,
      Country == "Thailand" ~ 17000,
      Country == "Myanmar" ~ 16000,
      Country == "India" ~ 15000,
      Country == "Philippines" ~ 13500,
      TRUE ~ Y1961
    ),
    right_y = case_when(
      Country == "Japan" ~ Y1980,
      Country == "Korea" ~ Y1980,
      Country == "China" ~ Y1980,
      Country == "Indonesia" ~ Y1980,
      Country == "Malaysia" ~ 29000,
      Country == "Myanmar" ~ 28000,
      Country == "SriLanka" ~ 27000,
      Country == "Philippines" ~ 23000,
      Country == "VietNam" ~ 22000,
      Country == "India" ~ 21000,
      Country == "Thailand" ~ 20000,
      TRUE ~ Y1980
    )
  )

ggplot(rice_wide) +
  
  # left grey guide lines
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = 1951, xend = 1961,
        y = left_y, yend = Y1961),
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  
  # right grey guide lines
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = 1980, xend = 1988,
        y = Y1980, yend = right_y),
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  
  # colored slope lines
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = 1961, xend = 1980,
        y = Y1961, yend = Y1980,
        color = Country),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  
  # value labels for 1961
  geom_text(
    aes(x = 1961, y = Y1961, label = round(Y1961, 0)),
    size = 3,
    hjust = 1.1,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  
  # value labels for 1980
  geom_text(
    aes(x = 1980, y = Y1980, label = round(Y1980, 0)),
    size = 3,
    hjust = -0.1,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  
  # country labels on the left
  geom_text(
    aes(x = 1950.5, y = left_y, label = Country),
    hjust = 1,
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  
  # country labels on the right
  geom_text(
    aes(x = 1988.5, y = right_y, label = Country),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1961, 1980),
    limits = c(1947, 1992)
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Rice Yield of Top 11 Asian Countries",
    subtitle = "1961-1980",
    caption = "Prepared by: Dr. Kam Tin Seong",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 13, hjust = 0),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.95),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", color = "grey30"),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 40, 20, 40)
  )

The original code uses newggslopegraph() from the CGPfunctions package to create a slope graph. However, this package is not available for my current version of R, so the function cannot be installed or loaded successfully. Therefore, I use ggplot2 as an alternative to recreate the same type of visualisation.

In this code, the rice yield data is first filtered to keep only the two selected years, 1961 and 1980. The data is then reshaped into a wide format so that each country has one yield value for 1961 and one yield value for 1980. The geom_segment() function is used to draw the coloured slope lines between the two years, while grey guide lines and text labels are added to reproduce the structure of the original slope graph.

```{r}
make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts, 
                        tz = tz[1],

  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))

}
```

```{r}
wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday',
```

## 17.5 Plotting Cycle Plot

## 17.5.1 Step 1: Data Import

```{r}
air <- read_excel("data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")
```

## 17.5.2 Step 2: Deriving month and year fields

```{r}
air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`), 
                    levels=1:12, 
                    labels=month.abb, 
                    ordered=TRUE) 
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))
```

## 17.5.3 Step 4: Extracting the target country

```{r}
Vietnam <- air %>% 
  select(`Vietnam`, 
         month, 
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)
```

## 17.5.4 Step 5: Computing year average arrivals by month

```{r}
hline.data <- Vietnam %>% 
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))
```

## 17.5.5 Srep 6: Plotting the cycle plot

```{r}
ggplot() + 
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year, 
                y=`Vietnam`, 
                group=month), 
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue), 
             data=hline.data, 
             linetype=6, 
             colour="red", 
             size=0.5) + 
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")
```

The original code uses `newggslopegraph()` from the `CGPfunctions` package to create a slope graph. However, this package is not available for my current version of R, so the function cannot be installed or loaded successfully. Therefore, I use `ggplot2` as an alternative to recreate the same type of visualisation.

In this code, the rice yield data is first filtered to keep only the two selected years, 1961 and 1980. The data is then reshaped into a wide format so that each country has one yield value for 1961 and one yield value for 1980. The `geom_segment()` function is used to draw the coloured slope lines between the two years, while grey guide lines and text labels are added to reproduce the structure of the original slope graph.
